Before the city learned to argue, Mara climbed to the roof with a chipped blue kettle and watered the garden no one had planted. Tomatoes leaned from cracked paint tins. Mint crowded an old drawer. Bees stumbled among them like tiny, drunken guests. She pretended not to need their company.

Her neighbors called the roof useless. Then winter came, and the street below tightened its collar against the wind. Mara kept climbing. Some mornings she found footprints beside hers, or a paper bag of seeds, or a note saying only, Try again. She kept every note beneath her thin pillow.

By spring, the roof had become a country. Someone brought a table. Someone else repaired the stairs. On Sundays they ate bread above the traffic, passing salt hand to hand, while laundry snapped behind them like bright flags surrendering to the weather. Nobody could remember who had begun it all.

Mara said little. She liked listening to names travel across the table, learning which silences belonged to grief and which to sleep. Sometimes she missed the lonely mornings, their clean arithmetic, one kettle, one woman, one impossible green thing insisting on more. Then someone would ask her for fresh basil.

Years later, when the building was sold and the garden carried away in strangers’ arms, Mara kept a single tomato seed in her coat pocket. It was not hope exactly. It was smaller, harder, and more willing to wait for weather. She closed her fingers around it and smiled softly.
